prompt.context: Your client is a startup in a small village in Italy that provides the local delivery of packages sent to this village through UPS's next-day-delivery service. The CEO of this firm has hired you to help them decide how many trucks to lease. There are different models available, but the client has been told that they will need to have a consistent fleet (they can only lease one model type), so we will also need to identify what model they should lease. The company operates as follows: (i) they receive every package at 5pm from UPS, (ii) a group of people sorts the packages, (iii) the packages are loaded on trucks and stored overnight, and (iv) delivery starts at 9am for 10 hours.
prompt.question: How would you suggest approaching the client's problem? Specifically, which truck model should the client lease and how many trucks will they need?

clarifying_info.q: How many packages are delivered per day?
What are the dimensions of a typical package?
How many days per week does the company operate?
How long does it take to deliver a single package?
clarifying_info.a: It takes 8 minutes on average to deliver a single package and be ready for the next one — assume they deliver one every 8 minutes.

clarifying_info.q: Should we consider driver, fuel, or other operational costs?
clarifying_info.a: No — drivers, fuel, etc. are not considered and do not make a material difference to the analysis for simplicity.
Three models: Truck A costs $150/day with dimensions 3x4x5; Truck B costs $40/day with dimensions 9x2x1; Truck C costs $130/day with dimensions 6x8x10.

framework: Analyze demand: determine total packages to deliver per day and average time per delivery
Calculate minimum trucks required based on time constraint (delivery hours in a day vs. time per package)
Evaluate each truck model: calculate capacity per truck, trucks needed, and total daily cost
Select the model with the lowest total daily cost that meets or exceeds the minimum truck constraint
Identify risks and potential profit growth opportunities

questions.prompt: Given 1,000 packages/day and 8 minutes per delivery over a 10-hour window, what is the minimum number of trucks needed based on the time constraint?
questions.guidance: The bottleneck is time: each truck can deliver one package every 8 minutes over a 10-hour (600-minute) window, so each truck delivers 600/8 = 75 packages/day. Total trucks needed = 1,000 / 75 = 13.3, so at minimum 14 trucks are required to deliver all packages within the time window.

math.setup: Minimum trucks = (time to deliver all packages) / (available delivery time per truck) = (8 min × 1,000 packages) / (10 hours × 60 min)

questions.prompt: For each truck model (A, B, C), calculate the capacity per truck, the number of trucks needed to carry all 1,000 packages, and the total daily cost. Which model should the client choose?
questions.guidance: Capacity = product of truck dimensions. Trucks needed = ceil(1,000 packages / capacity), but also must be at least 14 (the time-constraint minimum). Total cost = trucks needed × cost per day. Truck C has the lowest total daily cost at $1,820.

math.setup: Capacity per truck = length × width × height. Trucks needed = max(ceil(1,000 / capacity), 14). Total cost = trucks needed × cost per day.
steps: Truck C: capacity = 6×8×10 = 480; trucks = ceil(1,000/480) = 3, but time constraint requires 14; cost = 14 × $130 = $1,820
math.answer: Select Truck C: 14 trucks at $130/day = $1,820/day total — the lowest daily cost.

questions.prompt: Six months later the recommendation is successful. What risks should the CEO be assessing?
questions.guidance: Encourage an internal/external risk structure. Strong answers cover operational reliability, supplier concentration, competitive exposure, and macro/technology risks.

questions.prompt: Now explore sources of profit growth for this company with the constraint that no new trucks can be added and existing leases cannot be changed. Push for out-of-the-box solutions.
questions.guidance: Candidates should think across both the cost and revenue sides given the constraint on fleet size. Strong answers address underutilized truck capacity (time and space), diversified revenue streams, and cost structure optimization.

brainstorming.prompt: What risks should the CEO consider as the business scales? (Internal vs. External)

categories.name: Internal
ideas: Need for extra/backup drivers if employees get sick — do we have sufficient headcount?
Unionized drivers may push labor costs up in the future
Trucks can break down, causing late deliveries — need contingency or spare trucks
Insurance costs may be higher than forecasted
Drivers may receive more traffic fines than forecasted as they rush to meet delivery windows

categories.name: External
ideas: Single supplier concentration risk — client is captive to UPS
Adoption of digital communication (e-mail) could reduce package volumes over time
Government regulation changes affecting delivery operations
New competition entering the village — low barriers to entry since UPS could partner with any carrier meeting service metrics at lower cost
No brand association — UPS could switch to a competitor or launch its own last-mile operation

recommendation: Lease Truck C (dimensions 6×8×10, $130/day): 14 trucks are required to meet the time-based delivery constraint, yielding a total daily cost of $1,820 — the lowest of the three options

Truck C dominates because its large capacity means the binding constraint is time (14 trucks) not volume (only 3 trucks needed for volume), so its lower per-unit cost advantage compounds across fewer trucks than Truck A requires
risks: Sole dependence on UPS as the only package source exposes the business to supplier switching or margin pressure
Fleet reliability: breakdowns with a minimum-size fleet could cause SLA failures with no buffer trucks
Driver availability and potential labor cost escalation if workforce becomes unionized
next_steps: Negotiate multi-year lease terms for Truck C to lock in the $130/day rate
Explore additional revenue streams that leverage existing truck capacity (extended hours, pick-up services, third-party delivery contracts, truck-side advertising)
Develop contingency protocols for truck breakdowns and driver absenteeism
Assess feasibility of diversifying away from sole reliance on UPS
